title: Occupiers' liability
subtitle: Duties to visitors and trespassers under the 1957 and 1984 Acts
objectives: Identify who counts as an 'occupier' of premises, and explain why control — not ownership — is the decisive test
Distinguish the duty owed to lawful visitors under the 1957 Act from the duty owed to non-visitors under the 1984 Act
Apply the child-visitor and skilled-visitor modifications, and the limits on liability for warnings and obvious risks, to new fact patterns

leadingAuthorities.role: Statutory duty of care owed to lawful visitors
Narrower statutory duty owed to trespassers and other non-visitors
Defines 'occupier' by reference to control of premises, and confirms more than one person can occupy the same premises
Applies the child-visitor modification to an unforeseeable manner of injury from a foreseeable danger
Marks the limits of occupiers' duties where the risk is obvious and the visitor has become a trespasser by their own choice

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often treat 'occupier' as meaning 'owner' and treat the duty as a single fixed standard. Neither is right, and both mistakes cost marks. Where the profile shows knowledge ahead of application, this note appears: 'You know there are two Acts — this lesson is about working out, on the facts, who the occupier actually is and which Act applies to which claimant.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've handled the statutory definitions before. This lesson's test pool leans towards application: expect scenarios where you have to work out who the occupier is and whether the claimant is a visitor, before you even get to the standard of care.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Slow down through Parts 1 and 2 and be confident you can state the control test for 'occupier' and the basic content of the 1957 Act duty before moving on — the later parts on children, skilled visitors, and obvious risk all build on that foundation.

overview.hook: A rotten branch, a derelict boat, a flooded quarry, a hotel corridor. Four ordinary pieces of property, four very different questions about who was responsible for what happened on them — and in every case, the first thing a court has to work out isn't whether there was a danger, but who, in law, was in charge of the place at all.

parts.heading: Who is the 'occupier'? Control, not ownership
parts.voice: explanatory and methodical, building the test piece by piece before testing it
body: Occupiers' liability governs the duty owed by someone in control of premises for the state of those premises — as opposed to ordinary negligence, which governs what people do on them. The first question in any problem is deceptively simple: who is the occupier? Students default to 'the owner', and that is often wrong.

The test is control, not title. Whoever has a sufficient degree of control over premises to be expected to guard against dangers on them is the occupier, whatever the paperwork says. That means a tenant can be the occupier of a flat they don't own; a contractor can be the occupier of a site they're working on but don't own; and — critically — more than one person can be an occupier of the same premises at the same time, each owing a duty appropriate to the degree and kind of control they actually exercise.

Wheat v Lacon is the leading authority on exactly this point. A pub was owned by a brewery, which licensed a manager to live in and run it as a manager, not a tenant — meaning the brewery retained a significant degree of control over parts of the building, including a private staircase where the claimant's husband fell and died after being lawfully on the premises as a paying guest.

The House of Lords held that both the brewery and the manager could be occupiers simultaneously, each in respect of the degree of control each retained. The brewery, which retained the right to repair and maintain the structure, owed a duty in respect of the staircase's physical state; the manager's own conduct was a separate question. The lesson generalises: don't ask 'who owns this?' — ask 'who had control over this state of affairs, and over this particular danger?'

components.definition: A person with a sufficient degree of control over premises to be expected to guard against dangers on them. Control, not ownership or legal title, is decisive, and more than one person may be an occupier of the same premises at the same time in respect of different aspects of it.

components.factsShort: A brewery owned a pub run by a manager under a licence; the manager's wife took in the claimant's husband as a paying guest, who fell on a poorly lit private staircase and died.
components.ratioShort: More than one person can be an 'occupier' of the same premises at once, each owing a duty in proportion to the degree of control they retain over the relevant part or danger.

expanded.facts: Lacon & Co, brewers, owned a public house and employed a manager, Mr Richardson, to run it, with the family permitted to live upstairs. Mrs Richardson took in the Wheats as paying guests. Mr Wheat fell down a poorly lit back staircase — used to access the private accommodation — and was killed. The staircase's handrail was missing a section and the lighting had failed.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The House of Lords held that both Lacon & Co, as owners who retained the right and responsibility for structural repair, and the manager, in respect of his own day-to-day running of the premises, could each be an occupier for the purposes of the Act, in respect of the aspects of the premises they respectively controlled. On the facts, however, the brewery was not found liable, as the state of the staircase did not amount to a breach of the duty it owed.
expanded.significance: Wheat v Lacon is the standard authority that 'occupier' is a functional, control-based concept rather than a title-based one, and that liability can be split between multiple occupiers according to what each of them actually controlled — a point tested constantly in problem questions involving landlords, contractors, and licensees.

interaction.prompt: Under Wheat v Lacon, what is the correct test for identifying an 'occupier' of premises?
options: Whoever holds legal title to the land
Whoever has a sufficient degree of control over the premises to be expected to guard against dangers on them
Whoever is physically present most often
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — control, not ownership, is decisive, and it can be shared between more than one person over different aspects of the same premises.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — ownership is not the test. Wheat v Lacon establishes a control-based test, which is why an owner, a manager, and a contractor can each be an occupier of the same building at once, in respect of what each of them actually controls.

parts.heading: The 1957 Act: the duty owed to lawful visitors
parts.voice: plain and businesslike, presenting the statute as a working tool rather than a story
body: Once the occupier is identified, the next question is what kind of entrant the claimant was, because the two governing statutes set very different standards. The Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 covers 'visitors' — people the occupier has invited or permitted to be on the premises, including those with implied permission (the classic postman walking up a garden path) and those entering under a right conferred by law.

Section 2(2) sets the core standard: the occupier must take such care as in all the circumstances of the case is reasonable to see that the visitor will be reasonably safe in using the premises for the purposes for which they are invited or permitted to be there. Note the qualifier at the end — the duty is tied to the purpose of the visit. A visitor invited into the front hall is not automatically owed the same protection wandering into a locked plant room.

This is an ordinary negligence-style standard of reasonableness, not a guarantee of safety. An occupier who has taken reasonable care is not liable simply because an accident happened. The Act does, however, single out two categories for special treatment, because the ordinary 'reasonable visitor' assumption doesn't fit them: children, and people exercising a trade or calling on the premises.

components.text: The common duty of care is a duty to take such care as in all the circumstances of the case is reasonable to see that the visitor will be reasonably safe in using the premises for the purposes for which he is invited or permitted by the occupier to be there.
elements: A duty of reasonable care, not an absolute guarantee of safety
Assessed 'in all the circumstances of the case'
Tied to the purpose for which the visitor was invited or permitted onto the premises

components.text: The circumstances relevant for the present purpose include the degree of care, and of want of care, which would ordinarily be looked for in such a visitor, so that (for example) in proper cases — (a) an occupier must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults; and (b) an occupier may expect that a person, in the exercise of his calling, will appreciate and guard against any special risks ordinarily incident to it.
elements: The standard adjusts to the kind of visitor in question
Children: occupier must expect less care from them than from adults
Skilled visitors: occupier may expect them to guard against risks ordinary to their trade

interaction.prompt: Under s 2(2) of the 1957 Act, what must the occupier show to avoid liability to a lawful visitor who is injured on the premises?
options: That the premises were entirely free of any danger
That reasonable care was taken to see the visitor would be reasonably safe for the purpose of their visit
That the visitor signed a disclaimer before entering
interaction.explanation: The 1957 Act imposes a duty of reasonable care, tied to the purpose of the visit — not a strict guarantee that nothing will ever go wrong on the premises.

parts.heading: Children on the premises: Jolley v Sutton LBC
parts.voice: case-narrative, using one striking case to carry the whole doctrinal point
body: The s 2(3)(a) instruction — that occupiers must be prepared for children to be less careful than adults — sounds modest on paper. Jolley v Sutton LBC shows how far it can actually stretch, because it isn't only about children behaving carelessly; it's about children behaving inventively, in ways adults would not predict.

The council had left an abandoned, visibly rotting boat on a grassy area near a block of flats for around two years, despite its own staff twice noting it should be removed. Two teenage boys decided to 'repair' it, propped it up on a car jack, and were working underneath it when it collapsed, seriously injuring one of them.

The council's defence was that it could foresee children being hurt by, say, falling through the boat's rotten planking while playing on it — but not this: a lengthy, deliberate quasi-engineering project involving jacking the hull up and working underneath it. The Court of Appeal accepted that distinction and found for the council. The House of Lords reversed, restoring the trial judge's finding for the claimant.

The House of Lords' reasoning is the point to remember: it is enough that the boat was a known allurement to children, and that some form of physical injury from meddling with it was foreseeable — the occupier does not additionally have to foresee the exact way in which the child's ingenuity would bring the danger about. Foreseeability of the general kind of accident is enough; foreseeability of the precise mechanism is not required, and that principle sits especially firmly where children are the visitors in question.

components.caseName: Jolley v Sutton London Borough Council
components.factsShort: A council left a derelict, rotting boat on land near flats for around two years; two teenagers jacked it up to 'repair' it and one was seriously injured when it fell on him.
components.ratioShort: Where a danger to children is foreseeable in general terms, the occupier need not foresee the exact way in which a child's own ingenuity brings the injury about; children's characteristic inventiveness and lack of caution is itself part of what the occupier must guard against.

expanded.facts: A derelict cabin cruiser was abandoned on land owned by Sutton LBC, near a block of flats where children regularly played. Council staff twice recorded that it should be removed as a danger but it was not moved. Two 14-year-old boys decided to repair the boat, raised it on a car jack to work underneath the hull, and it slipped and crushed one of them, causing severe spinal injury.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Hoffmann, giving the leading speech, held that the trial judge had been entitled to find the accident foreseeable: it was foreseeable that children would meddle with the boat and suffer some physical injury as a result, even though the specific mechanism — being crushed while working underneath a jacked-up hull — had not been anticipated by anyone. The law does not require an occupier (or any defendant in negligence) to foresee the precise sequence of events, only the general type and kind of accident.
expanded.significance: Jolley is the leading illustration of how far the child-visitor modification extends: it is not simply that children may be careless, but that their capacity for unpredictable, inventive engagement with an allurement is itself foreseeable in general terms, which lowers the bar for establishing the danger was one the occupier ought to have guarded against.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario most likely to trigger the enhanced child-visitor duty, applying Jolley v Sutton.
interaction.scenarioText: A school leaves an old, disused climbing frame with visibly rusted joints in a fenced play area for two years, despite a staff memo flagging it for removal. A ten-year-old pupil climbs onto the top bar during break time and a joint gives way, causing her to fall.
tappableSpans: disused climbing frame with visibly rusted joints
fenced play area for two years
staff memo flagging it for removal
interaction.correctSpan: disused climbing frame with visibly rusted joints
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the allurement-plus-danger combination Jolley turns on: a known, deteriorating hazard left accessible to children, where some form of physical injury from their interacting with it is foreseeable in general terms, whatever the precise way it happens.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on the state of the object itself, not the surrounding facts about time or memos — Jolley's key move is recognising a visibly dangerous, alluring object as foreseeably risky to children in a general sense.

parts.heading: Skilled visitors, warnings, and obvious risk: Tomlinson v Congleton
parts.voice: argumentative, presenting the tempting broad reading of the duty and then cutting it down
body: It's easy to read the 1957 Act as imposing a broad, protective duty and assume occupiers are usually on the hook when something goes wrong. Two features of the law push hard the other way, and Tomlinson v Congleton is the case that shows both operating at once.

First, s 2(3)(b): an occupier may expect a person exercising a trade or calling to appreciate and guard against risks ordinary to that trade. A roofer coming to fix a roof is expected to know about the risk of falling from height in a way an ordinary visitor is not; the occupier doesn't need to warn a professional about the obvious hazards of their own profession.

Second, and more sweepingly, the 1957 Act contains no duty in respect of risks willingly accepted, and courts have consistently held that occupiers owe no duty to warn of, or safeguard against, risks that are obvious. Congleton Borough Council owned a country park with a lake formed from a former sand quarry. Swimming was expressly prohibited by prominent signage, but people did it anyway; the council knew this and had even discussed, but not funded, planting reeds to deter swimmers. Mr Tomlinson, an adult, dived into shallow water, struck his head on the sandy bottom, and was rendered tetraplegic.

The House of Lords held the council owed no duty. The danger — shallow water and a risk of diving injury — was perfectly obvious to any adult; Tomlinson was not a visitor at all once he entered the water in defiance of the prohibition (he became, in effect, a trespasser for that activity), and even setting that aside, there is no duty to protect visitors against risks they have willingly and knowingly run, particularly where the 'danger' arises not from the state of the premises but from the claimant's own choice of activity on them. Lord Hoffmann was blunt about the social cost of expanding the duty: turning every natural hazard into a source of liability would pressure occupiers to fence off or destroy amenities that most people enjoy responsibly, for the sake of a minority who ignore an obvious risk.

components.label: Where the 1957/1984 duty runs out
points: Skilled visitors: an occupier may expect a visitor exercising a trade to appreciate and guard against risks ordinary to that trade (s 2(3)(b))
Obvious risks: there is generally no duty to warn of, or protect against, a risk that is obvious to the visitor

Willingly accepted risks: no duty arises in respect of risks the visitor has knowingly and willingly chosen to run, especially through their own choice of activity rather than the state of the premises itself
Warnings can discharge the duty under s 2(4) where, in all the circumstances, the warning was enough to make the visitor reasonably safe

components.factsShort: An adult visitor dived into a shallow lake in a country park despite prominent no-swimming signs, struck the sandy bottom, and was left tetraplegic.
components.ratioShort: Occupiers owe no duty to warn of or guard against obvious risks, and no duty arises from a visitor's willing acceptance of a risk associated with their own chosen activity rather than the state of the premises.

expanded.facts: Congleton BC maintained a country park including a lake formed from a disused quarry. Swimming was banned by clear signage due to known risks of shallow water and underwater hazards, and lifeguards patrolled to warn people off, but swimming continued to be common. Tomlinson, aged 18, ran into the water and dived, striking the sloping sandy bottom and suffering a severe spinal injury leaving him tetraplegic.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The House of Lords held the council owed no duty. The risk of diving into shallow water was obvious; there was no danger due to the state of the premises beyond what any adult would appreciate, and the injury arose from Tomlinson's own choice to dive rather than any unusual hazard the council had failed to address. Lord Hoffmann emphasised the social cost of a wider duty: councils would be driven to close or spoil public amenities to guard against risks that responsible visitors do not run.
expanded.significance: Tomlinson is the leading modern statement that occupiers' liability does not convert every natural or obvious hazard into a source of liability, and that a visitor's free choice to engage in a risky activity — as opposed to being exposed to an unexpected danger in the premises themselves — will very often defeat the claim outright.

interaction.prompt: In which scenario is an occupier more likely to escape liability on obvious-risk grounds, applying Tomlinson?
interaction.scenarioA: A visitor climbs over a locked fence marked 'danger — deep water, no access' and dives into a reservoir from a height, striking rocks below the surface that were not visible from the bank.
interaction.scenarioB: A visitor slips on an unmarked patch of black ice that has formed overnight on the occupier's usual pedestrian entrance path, which the occupier knew was prone to icing and had not gritted.
interaction.explanation: A mirrors Tomlinson: an obvious, signposted risk that the visitor chose to run despite a clear warning and physical barrier. B is closer to an ordinary breach of the standard duty of care — an unaddressed, non-obvious hazard on a route visitors are expected to use, which the occupier knew about.

parts.heading: Non-visitors: the narrower 1984 Act duty
parts.voice: Socratic, posing the trespasser problem before resolving it with the statutory test
body: Here's the hard question the 1957 Act deliberately leaves unanswered: what does an occupier owe to someone who has no permission to be there at all — a trespasser, or someone exceeding the scope of permission they did have? Common sense says something less than the full common duty of care; historically, the law went further and said almost nothing at all, treating trespassers as owed only a duty not to cause deliberate or reckless harm.

Parliament corrected that with the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984, which creates a duty to non-visitors, but only where three conditions are all met: the occupier is aware of the danger, or has reasonable grounds to believe it exists; the occupier knows, or has reasonable grounds to believe, that someone is in the vicinity of the danger or may come into it; and the risk is one against which, in all the circumstances, the occupier may reasonably be expected to offer some protection. Even then, the resulting duty — to take such care as is reasonable to see the non-visitor does not suffer injury on the premises by reason of the danger — is narrower than the 1957 Act standard, and is explicitly capable of being discharged by a warning, in circumstances where a warning to a lawful visitor might not be enough.

So which Act applies is not a side issue — it's often the whole case. Someone who wanders past a clearly marked boundary onto a construction site is almost certainly a trespasser owed, at most, the narrower 1984 duty. Someone invited to a shop who wanders from the sales floor into a marked 'staff only' stockroom has exceeded the scope of their permission and may likewise have become a non-visitor for that part of the premises, even though they entered lawfully in the first place — the same person can be a visitor in one room and a trespasser in the next.

components.text: An occupier of premises owes a duty to another (not being his visitor) in respect of any such risk as is referred to in subsection (1) above if — (a) he is aware of the danger or has reasonable grounds to believe that it exists; (b) he knows or has reasonable grounds to believe that the other is in the vicinity of the danger concerned or that he may come into the vicinity of the danger; and (c) the risk is one against which, in all the circumstances of the case, he may reasonably be expected to offer the other some protection.
elements: Occupier's actual or constructive knowledge of the danger
Occupier's actual or constructive knowledge the non-visitor is or may come near it
The risk is one the occupier may reasonably be expected to guard against in all the circumstances

interaction.prompt: Put these steps in the order a court works through the 1984 Act duty to a non-visitor.
items: Confirm the claimant is a non-visitor rather than a lawful visitor
Ask whether the occupier knew, or had reasonable grounds to believe, the danger existed
Ask whether the occupier knew, or had reasonable grounds to believe, the non-visitor was or might come near the danger
Ask whether the risk is one the occupier could reasonably be expected to offer protection against
Assess whether reasonable care was taken, noting a warning may be sufficient to discharge the duty
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the structure of s 1(3): identify non-visitor status first, then work through the three knowledge-and-reasonableness conditions before reaching the (narrower) content of the duty itself.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Reorder around the statute: confirm non-visitor status, then the occupier's knowledge of the danger, then their knowledge of the claimant's proximity to it, then whether protection was reasonably to be expected, and only then the standard actually owed.

testPool.prompt: What is the legal test for identifying the 'occupier' of premises for the purposes of occupiers' liability?
acceptableAnswers: who has control, not who owns it
testPool.modelAnswer: The occupier is whoever has a sufficient degree of control over the premises to be expected to guard against dangers on them — control, not ownership, is decisive, and more than one person can be an occupier at once.

testPool.prompt: Which Act governs the duty owed to lawful visitors to premises?
options: Occupiers' Liability Act 1957
Occupiers' Liability Act 1984

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the three conditions for a duty to arise under s 1(3) of the 1984 Act?
options: The occupier knows or has reasonable grounds to believe the danger exists
The occupier knows or has reasonable grounds to believe the non-visitor is or may come near the danger
The non-visitor must have entered the premises within the last 24 hours
The risk is one the occupier could reasonably be expected to offer some protection against
testPool.trapExplanation: There is no time limit built into the 1984 Act test. The three real conditions are about the occupier's knowledge of the danger, knowledge of the non-visitor's proximity to it, and the reasonableness of expecting protection — not the timing of entry.

testPool.prompt: Under s 2(3)(b) of the 1957 Act, what may an occupier expect of a visitor exercising a trade or calling on the premises?
options: That they will appreciate and guard against risks ordinarily incident to that trade
That they carry their own insurance
That they will always refuse to work if any risk is present

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, adapted from Jolley v Sutton LBC, highlight the sentence stating the ratio on foreseeability and children.
testPool.passage: The council could not have predicted the exact way the boys chose to interfere with the boat. But it is enough that some form of physical injury to a child meddling with the dangerous, alluring object was foreseeable in general terms; the law does not require the occupier to foresee the precise mechanism by which a child's ingenuity brings the danger about.
testPool.ratioSentence: But it is enough that some form of physical injury to a child meddling with the dangerous, alluring object was foreseeable in general terms; the law does not require the occupier to foresee the precise mechanism by which a child's ingenuity brings the danger about.

testPool.prompt: Order the analytical steps in an occupiers' liability problem question.
items: Identify who has sufficient control to be the occupier
Determine whether the claimant is a visitor or a non-visitor
Identify which Act (1957 or 1984) sets the applicable duty
Apply the relevant statutory duty, including any modifications for children or skilled visitors
Consider whether a warning or the obviousness of the risk defeats or discharges the duty

testPool.prompt: A landlord retains the freehold of a block of flats and is contractually responsible for maintaining the communal stairwell, while individual flats are let to tenants who control the interiors. A visitor is injured by a broken stairwell handrail. Who is the likely occupier for this purpose?
options: The landlord, in respect of the communal stairwell it retains responsibility for maintaining
Only the tenant whose flat the visitor was visiting
Nobody — occupiers' liability does not apply to communal areas
testPool.explanation: Applying Wheat v Lacon, control over the relevant part of the premises is what matters. The landlord retains control of, and responsibility for, the communal stairwell, making it the likely occupier for a danger located there, even though it does not control the individual flats.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that is most likely to defeat a claim on obvious-risk grounds, applying Tomlinson v Congleton.
testPool.scenarioText: A visitor to a park sees a clearly marked sign reading 'steep drop — keep to path' at the edge of a cliff walk, steps past the sign onto the loose edge to take a photograph, and falls.
tappableSpans: clearly marked sign reading 'steep drop — keep to path'
steps past the sign onto the loose edge
testPool.correctSpan: clearly marked sign reading 'steep drop — keep to path'
testPool.feedbackCorrect: That's the key fact: a clear warning of an obvious danger. Under Tomlinson, an occupier is not liable where a visitor knowingly disregards an obvious risk that has been flagged, especially where the resulting harm flows from the visitor's own choice.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on the warning itself rather than the visitor's later choice — the presence of a clear sign flagging an obvious danger is what most directly supports the occupier escaping liability under Tomlinson.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario better illustrates the child-visitor modification in s 2(3)(a), as applied in Jolley v Sutton?
testPool.scenarioA: An adult trespasser breaks into a fenced building site at night and is injured falling into a marked excavation.
testPool.scenarioB: A council leaves a broken, half-collapsed shed on open land near a primary school for months; children dismantle parts of it to build a den and one is injured when a wall section falls on them.
testPool.explanation: B mirrors Jolley: a known, deteriorating hazard left accessible near children, where the exact way children engage with it (building a den, dismantling it) need not be precisely foreseen — general foreseeability of some physical injury from meddling is enough. A raises trespasser and 1984 Act issues, not the child-visitor modification.

testPool.prompt: A qualified electrician is called to fix faulty wiring and is injured by touching a live wire he had been specifically warned about and which is an ordinary risk of his trade. Is the occupier likely liable under s 2(3)(b)?
options: Unlikely — the occupier may expect a tradesperson to appreciate and guard against risks ordinary to their trade
Certain — occupiers are always liable for injuries to visitors regardless of their profession

testPool.prompt: A disused rail yard owned by a rail company is surrounded by a damaged fence with a well-used gap that local teenagers regularly use as a shortcut, which staff have reported but not repaired for over a year. A 15-year-old is injured climbing on a stationary freight wagon after entering through the gap. Analyse the rail company's likely liability.
factsToOrder: The teenager entered through a known, unrepaired gap in the fence
Staff had reported the gap and the shortcut use over a year earlier
The teenager was not invited or permitted onto the site — a non-visitor
The teenager was injured climbing on a stationary wagon
The danger (climbing on wagons) was one the company could anticipate given known trespasser use

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the rail company, as occupier, owes a duty to the teenager under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 given his status as a non-visitor.
modelAnswer.rule: Under s 1(3) of the 1984 Act, a duty to a non-visitor arises where the occupier is aware, or has reasonable grounds to believe, that a danger exists; knows or has reasonable grounds to believe a person is or may come near it; and the risk is one the occupier may reasonably be expected to offer some protection against.
modelAnswer.application: The company had actual knowledge of the danger area (stationary wagons) and, through the reported unrepaired fence gap and known pattern of teenagers using it as a shortcut, had reasonable grounds to believe non-visitors were likely to be in the vicinity of the danger. Given over a year's notice and the known, regular use of the gap, it is arguable the company could reasonably have been expected to offer some protection, whether by repairing the fence or otherwise restricting access to the wagons.
modelAnswer.conclusion: A duty under the 1984 Act is likely to arise on these facts, and the failure to repair a known, long-standing breach used regularly by young trespassers is likely to amount to a breach of the narrower duty owed to non-visitors.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best explains the House of Lords' reasoning in Tomlinson v Congleton for finding no duty was owed?
options: Because Tomlinson was under 18 at the time and children cannot claim under the 1957 Act
Because the risk of diving into shallow water was obvious, and the injury arose from Tomlinson's own free choice to run a known risk rather than from an unusual danger in the state of the premises
Because the council had never discussed any measures to deter swimming
testPool.trapExplanation: Tomlinson was an adult (18), so the child-visitor point is a red herring, and the council had in fact discussed deterrent measures without implementing them — that detail supports awareness of the issue, not the reason no duty was owed. The real reasoning turns on obviousness of the risk and the claimant's own free choice.

testPool.prompt: Can the same person be a lawful visitor in one part of a building and a trespasser in another part of the same building?
options: Yes — permission is scope-limited, so exceeding the area or purpose of an invitation can turn a visitor into a non-visitor for that part
No — once someone is a lawful visitor they remain one throughout the entire building

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The recurring mistake in this lesson is skipping straight to 'was there a danger and was it dangerous enough' without first pinning down who the occupier is and whether the claimant counts as a visitor at all — get either of those wrong and the wrong Act, and the wrong duty, gets applied to the whole answer.
